passage:
Tushar's joke about the city bus service spread far beyond his friends overnight, and not kindly. By morning thousands of strangers were calling him names, and someone had posted his old photo from a college play with a mocking caption. His hands shook on the phone. Under the noise he felt worthless and afraid: one message claimed they knew his office.

Manoj saw it and did not post a defence. He wrote privately: "That looks awful. What would help? I can read the messages for you if you want." Tushar answered, "Yes. Please just stay on a call." Manoj stayed on for an hour, saying little, and did not pile on advice.

Tushar muted his notifications, took screenshots of the threats and reported them, and told his manager and two friends. He posted one line correcting a wrong fact about his job, then went quiet.

Among the flood was a note from Sudha: "Your joke landed on people who rely on that bus. I think it was careless." It stung, but it was fair. Next day he replied calmly: "You are right. I am sorry for the tone." He answered none of the insults. Over the following week the storm moved on to something else.

qa.q: What was attached to the mocking caption?
qa.a: It was attached to his old photo from a college play.

qa.q: How did Manoj's response differ from the crowd's, and how did Tushar treat Sudha's note compared with the insults?
qa.a: The crowd piled on, while Manoj wrote privately, asked what would help and stayed on the call without advice. Tushar answered Sudha's fair point calmly and left the insults unanswered.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he read the message claiming they knew his office?
qa.a: He felt afraid and worthless, and his hands shook.

qa.q: What steps did Tushar take to protect himself?
qa.a: He muted notifications, screenshotted and reported the threats, told his manager and two friends, and corrected one wrong fact once before going quiet.

grounding: One person's post goes viral, bringing fear and shame from a mob, a private friend's steady help, and one fair criticism that stands out from the abuse.

passage:
Afreen's Dada was in the hospital, and her stomach was full of stones. Nobody told her anything. On the third day she asked her father Farhan, "Is Dada going to die?" Farhan crouched down. "He is very ill. The doctors are working hard, and I do not know how it will go." It was scary, but less scary than the silence. She drew the two of them flying a kite and taped it beside his bed.

Dr Vijay explained the drip and the oxygen in simple words, and showed her the screen where the heartbeat was a green line. Afreen asked what each thing did. Knowing a little, she trusted the doctors more, and she prepared herself that it might not be enough.

It was not. Dada died on a Thursday. Afreen felt empty, then furious at the hospital, then confused. She cried in the car, asked why, and at the prayers she listened to her uncles telling stories about him. Some days the sadness came like waves, and she let it.

Weeks later her Dadi lay resting in the afternoons. Afreen pulled a chair beside the bed and read comic stories aloud. She did not try to fix anything. Dadi patted her hand and closed her eyes, smiling.

qa.q: What did Afreen draw for Dada?
qa.a: She drew the two of them flying a kite.

qa.q: How did honest answers change Afreen's fear, and how did her part with Dadi differ?
qa.a: Being told honestly and hearing simple explanations made the fear smaller and let her trust the doctors, though she prepared for bad news. With Dadi she did not need to fix anything, only read aloud and be there.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling on the third day when nobody told her anything?
qa.a: She felt afraid. Her stomach was full of stones and the silence scared her.

qa.q: What helped Afreen with her fear while Dada was in the hospital?
qa.a: She asked her father an honest question, asked Dr Vijay what each thing did, and drew a picture to tape beside his bed.

grounding: One child moves through fear for a hospitalised grandfather, trust in his doctors, grief after his death, and quiet love for a resting grandmother.

passage:
Disha kept replaying a game level in her head during maths, and when the bell rang for games time she would rather have stayed at the tablet. Her mother, Jaya, noticed she got upset whenever she was told to stop. They agreed on a timer and outdoor play after dinner, and Disha found she could stop when it rang.

She and her friend Jagdish were racing for the top of the class leaderboard. When Jagdish moved ahead, Disha sulked and deleted his chat message. Then she thought: it is only a score. She took a break, walked round the building, and later typed, "Rematch tomorrow? Good game." Jagdish sent back a thumbs-up.

The game kept flashing offers: "Get the golden armour!" Disha wanted it to look cool. She asked Jaya first, who said not for now and explained that the game is made to tempt. Disha remembered that Jagdish never cared what she wore in the game.

After one bad loss, a stranger wrote, "You okay? Tough round." Disha felt warm at that. She wrote "thanks, I'm okay" and nothing about where she lived or her school, then told Jaya about it.

qa.q: What did Disha type to Jagdish after her break?
qa.a: She typed, "Rematch tomorrow? Good game."

qa.q: How did Jaya respond when Disha got upset about stopping, compared with when Disha wanted the golden armour?
qa.a: When Disha got upset at being told to stop, Jaya agreed on a timer and outdoor play after dinner; when Disha asked about the armour, Jaya said not for now and explained that the game is made to tempt.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when Jagdish moved ahead on the leaderboard?
qa.a: She felt sulky and jealous, so she deleted his chat message before taking a break.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Disha to ask Jaya before buying the golden armour?
qa.a: The game is made to tempt, and Jaya could say no for now and explain why.

grounding: One child's time with an online game includes being unable to stop, a fierce rank race with a friend, purchase offers, and a stranger's kind message.

passage:
Kavitha heard her parents whispering behind the kitchen door: Papa's medicines, the shop rent, the school fees. She lay awake with worry until she asked her mother straight out, "What is happening?" Amma sat with her, explained in plain words what she could, and promised to keep her posted. Kavitha began tutoring a neighbour's boy for an hour after school, and still kept her own study slot and her Sunday cricket.

Watching Amma skip lunches to pay the fees, Kavitha felt thankful and heavy at the same time. "Thank you for everything," she said one night, and took on the washing-up and the shopping list. But when Amma said, "You must get top marks, for us," Kavitha replied, "I will work hard, and I may choose my own course." They were both quiet, and then Amma nodded.

At school, Farhan turned down every birthday invitation. "Busy," he said. The truth was that his mother's shop had closed, and every excuse cost him. Asif noticed and, without asking why, lent him class notes, sat with him in the library and never mentioned it to anyone. One day Farhan said, "We are short on money." Asif nodded. "Thanks for telling me." Farhan felt lighter.

qa.q: What did Kavitha start doing after school?
qa.a: She began tutoring a neighbour's boy for an hour.

qa.q: How did Kavitha's way of coping with worry differ from Farhan's, and how did Asif's help differ from gossip?
qa.a: Kavitha asked her mother directly, took a small job and kept studying. Farhan hid his situation and refused invitations until he told one friend. Asif quietly lent notes and company and told no one.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he kept answering "Busy" to birthday invitations?
qa.a: He was ashamed of the money trouble and afraid of being found out.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do if she feels she must repay her parents by giving up her own plans?
qa.a: She can say thanks and take fair responsibility at home, and tell her parents she may choose her own course, as she did.

grounding: Illness and money trouble at home bring one teenager worry and gratitude, another shame and hiding, and a third quiet, gossip-free help.

passage:
Darshan tied his shoelaces all by himself before school, tongue poking out. Papa hugged him. "I'm proud of you." Darshan felt warm all the way to the gate and ready to try the next thing.

In class, the teacher looked at his painting of a boat. "Well done, you tried so hard on those waves!" and pressed a gold star on his shirt. Darshan felt tall. Thomas, at the next desk, frowned. "You are not that good." Darshan's smile wobbled. He felt puzzled and a bit sad. He said, "I liked painting the waves," and did not brag. Thomas scuffed a shoe against the table leg and said nothing more.

Later, Yogesh held up a dinosaur made of clay. "Your dinosaur is so good!" said Darshan, and he meant it. "Can you teach me the spikes?" Yogesh beamed and showed him how to roll tiny pieces of clay, one by one.

qa.q: What did the teacher press on Darshan's shirt?
qa.a: The teacher pressed a gold star on his shirt.

qa.q: How did Thomas react to Darshan's gold star, compared with how Yogesh reacted to Darshan's praise?
qa.a: Thomas frowned, said "You are not that good" and then scuffed a shoe and said nothing more, while Yogesh beamed and showed Darshan how to roll tiny pieces of clay for the spikes.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when Thomas said "You are not that good"?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and a bit sad. His smile wobbled.

qa.q: What was a wise next step for Darshan after admiring Yogesh's dinosaur?
qa.a: Asking Yogesh to teach him the spikes was wise, since it turned admiration into learning.

grounding: A young child's day shows a parent's pride, a teacher's praise for effort, a classmate's frown at that praise, and his own admiration of a friend's work.

passage:
Dhruv sent the client the wrong price sheet and realised an hour later. His stomach dropped, and he feared Jaya, the manager, would give up on him. He walked into Seema's cabin. "I have made a serious mistake. Here is what happened, and here is a corrected sheet. Can you help me tell Jaya?"

Seema's first thought was to fix it quietly and say nothing. Her second was irritation: she could redo the whole report in an hour herself. She took a breath. A little cover might help today, but Dhruv would never learn from it. "You send the correction to the client and tell Jaya yourself. I will sit in." Dhruv did, voice shaky. Jaya thanked him for speaking up quickly and asked about next steps.

Yet after the meeting Seema doubted herself. She had handed Dhruv the entire big task with one hurried briefing. That evening she reread her instructions and saw the gaps. Next day she split the task into three parts, with a check-in after each. When Dhruv fumbled the first, she kept her hands off the keyboard and only asked, "What would you try?" By Friday he had finished part two cleanly.

qa.q: What did Dhruv send to the client by mistake?
qa.a: He sent the wrong price sheet.

qa.q: How did Seema's first impulses differ from what she actually did?
qa.a: She wanted to cover the mistake or take the task back, but instead she had Dhruv tell Jaya himself and sat in, then fixed her own briefing and delegated again in smaller steps.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he walked into Seema's cabin?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid that Jaya would give up on him.

qa.q: What made the smaller check-ins work for Seema and Dhruv?
qa.a: Splitting the task into three parts with a check-in after each let Seema guide without taking over, and Dhruv could finish part two cleanly.

grounding: A junior's serious mistake shows the junior's shame, a senior's urge to cover or take over, and her doubt about delegating that she repairs with smaller steps.
